title: GPU Not Detected (CUDA / Driver / PyTorch Mismatch)
description: Troubleshooting and resolving framework failure to detect available GPUs. This guide provides a structured flow to resolve driver, CUDA toolkit, and PyTorch/TensorFlow binary version mismatches.
name: GPU Not Detected (CUDA / Driver / PyTorch Mismatch)

quick_identification.description: PyTorch cannot access any CUDA device.

quick_identification.check: nvidia-smi shows GPUs but framework reports none
quick_identification.description: Hardware is visible to the driver but not to the ML framework.

quick_identification.check: Training falls back to CPU with device='cpu'
quick_identification.description: Workload executes on CPU despite GPU hardware presence.

symptoms.description: torch.cuda.is_available() or tf.config.list_physical_devices('GPU') returns empty or False.
symptoms.error_message: No explicit error; silent fallback to CPU.
symptoms.where_appears: Training script initialization, device selection code.

symptoms.description: nvidia-smi lists GPUs with a valid driver version, but the framework cannot see them.
symptoms.error_message: No explicit error; disconnect between system and framework visibility.
symptoms.where_appears: Environment setup, container runtime, virtual environment.

symptoms.description: Runtime fails with missing libcudart.so or libcuda.so shared libraries.
symptoms.error_message: ImportError: libcuda.so.1: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory.

symptoms.description: Framework reports CUDA version mismatch or incompatible runtime behavior.
symptoms.error_message: The NVIDIA driver on your system is too old or CUDA error: no kernel image is available.

root_causes.explanation: The framework wheel was compiled against a different CUDA toolkit version than the runtime libraries available on the system, breaking binary compatibility at libcudart or related linkage points.
recognition_clues: torch.version.cuda does not match the expected CUDA build.
nvidia-smi driver version and framework build metadata disagree.
The environment was installed via pip or conda without a pinned CUDA-specific package set.
root_causes.typical_environment: Conda environments, pip installs on shared clusters, manual PyPI installations.

root_causes.cause: NVIDIA Driver Too Old for CUDA Toolkit
root_causes.explanation: The installed driver does not satisfy the minimum version required by the CUDA runtime expected by the framework, so the runtime cannot initialize GPU execution.
recognition_clues: Driver version shown by nvidia-smi is below the documented minimum.
The error explicitly says the driver is too old.
The host uses a conservative OS repository driver package.
root_causes.typical_environment: Enterprise Linux distributions, long-running servers, VM images with stale drivers.

root_causes.cause: Missing or Broken NVIDIA Container Runtime
root_causes.explanation: Containerized workloads cannot see /dev/nvidia* devices unless the NVIDIA container runtime or equivalent GPU passthrough is configured, so the framework can only enumerate CPU devices.
recognition_clues: nvidia-smi works on the host but not inside the container.
GPU flags were omitted from the container invocation.
The container runtime is plain runc rather than the NVIDIA-enabled path.
root_causes.typical_environment: Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD runners, GPU-enabled container images.

root_causes.cause: Missing cuDNN or CUDA Shared Libraries
root_causes.explanation: The framework imports successfully but cannot load required runtime libraries, causing either explicit ImportError or silent fallback when the GPU backend cannot initialize.
recognition_clues: ldd on framework libraries shows missing CUDA-related .so files.
TensorFlow reports no GPU devices despite a CUDA build.
Base images are minimal and omit runtime libraries.
root_causes.typical_environment: Stripped-down Docker images, custom CUDA installs, minimal OS images.

root_causes.explanation: WSL2 depends on Windows-host driver support and a compatible userspace CUDA path; standard Linux driver assumptions do not apply cleanly.
recognition_clues: GPU is visible on the Windows host but not inside WSL2.
WSL2 lacks the expected CUDA library path or kernel-facing support.
The installed driver is not WSL2-capable.
root_causes.typical_environment: Windows development workstations, WSL2-based ML workflows.

root_causes.explanation: The process cannot access /dev/nvidia* due to device permissions, so device enumeration fails even though the driver is present.
recognition_clues: nvidia-smi works as root but fails as the user.
Device nodes have restrictive permissions.
The user is missing the expected device-access group.
root_causes.typical_environment: Shared servers, HPC clusters, restricted containers.

root_causes.explanation: The GPU exists at the driver layer but is not reliably initialized at the hardware link or power-management layer, so framework initialization fails after device discovery.
recognition_clues: nvidia-smi shows error states, N/A fields, or intermittent device visibility.
Kernel logs show PCIe or NVIDIA initialization errors.
The issue appears after suspend/resume or chassis maintenance.
root_causes.typical_environment: Desktop workstations, systems after hardware changes, nodes with unstable power management.

investigation_checklist.description: Verify driver version, GPU visibility, and GPU memory state.
Run torch.version.cuda or TensorFlow build metadata to identify the compiled CUDA target.
Compare driver version against NVIDIA-supported minimums for the target CUDA runtime.
Verify GPU passthrough is enabled in Docker or Kubernetes.
Use ldd on framework libraries to find missing CUDA or cuDNN dependencies.
Verify user has read/write access to GPU device files.
Confirm WSL2-capable NVIDIA driver support on the Windows host.

diagnostic_commands.command: python -c "import torch; print(f'CUDA available: {torch.cuda.is_available()}'); print(f'CUDA version: {torch.version.cuda}'); print(f'cuDNN: {torch.backends.cudnn.version()}')"
diagnostic_commands.expected_output: CUDA available: True, matching CUDA version, non-None cuDNN version.
diagnostic_commands.interpretation: False or version mismatch indicates binary incompatibility.

diagnostic_commands.expected_output: List of GPU devices, True for CUDA build.
diagnostic_commands.interpretation: Empty list or False indicates build or runtime issue.

diagnostic_commands.command: ldd $(python -c "import torch; import os; print(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(torch.__file__), 'lib', 'libtorch_python.so'))") | grep "not found"
diagnostic_commands.interpretation: Missing libraries indicate incomplete CUDA or cuDNN installation.

diagnostic_commands.expected_output: Driver version string and NVIDIA kernel modules loaded.
diagnostic_commands.interpretation: Missing nvidia_uvm can prevent CUDA runtime initialization.

diagnostic_tests.test: Compare nvidia-smi driver version against NVIDIA compatibility tables.
diagnostic_tests.expected_result: Driver version meets or exceeds the minimum required for the framework’s CUDA build.
diagnostic_tests.interpretation: If the driver is too old, upgrade the driver or reinstall the framework with a matching CUDA build.
diagnostic_tests.next_action: Install a newer NVIDIA driver or reinstall the framework with the correct CUDA channel.

diagnostic_tests.test: Run nvidia-smi inside the container versus on the host.
diagnostic_tests.interpretation: Failure indicates missing container runtime configuration.
diagnostic_tests.next_action: Install nvidia-container-toolkit and restart the Docker daemon.

diagnostic_tests.test: Run a minimal PyTorch tensor operation on GPU.
diagnostic_tests.command: python -c "import torch; x = torch.randn(10, 10).cuda(); print(x @ x)"
diagnostic_tests.interpretation: A runtime error indicates driver, library, or hardware initialization failure.
diagnostic_tests.next_action: Check kernel logs for NVIDIA driver errors if this fails.

decision_tree.question: Does nvidia-smi work on the host?

yes.question: Does a minimal CUDA tensor operation succeed?

yes.result: GPU is functional; issue is in application code.

no.result: Runtime CUDA error — check kernel logs and library linkage.

yes.question: Does docker run --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.1-base nvidia-smi work?

yes.result: Container runtime is OK; framework CUDA version mismatch — reinstall the framework with matching CUDA.

no.result: NVIDIA Container Toolkit is not installed or misconfigured.

yes.result: Permission issue or missing cuDNN — check /dev/nvidia* permissions and missing libraries.

no.result: Framework built for the wrong CUDA version — reinstall with the correct CUDA channel.

no.question: Is this a physical server or VM?

yes.result: Hardware or driver installation issue — reinstall NVIDIA driver, check PCIe seating.

no.result: GPU passthrough is not configured — enable PCI passthrough in the hypervisor.

solutions.solution: Reinstall PyTorch with Correct CUDA Version
solutions.quick_fix: Uninstall current PyTorch and reinstall with the matching CUDA index URL.
solutions.permanent_fix: Pin CUDA version in environment specifications and use lockfiles.
steps: Run python -c "import torch; print(torch.version.cuda)" to identify the expected CUDA build.
Run nvcc --version or nvidia-smi to identify system capability.
Uninstall current PyTorch packages.
Reinstall with the matching CUDA-specific index URL.
Verify torch.cuda.is_available().
tradeoffs: Can conflict with packages expecting a different PyTorch build.
solutions.performance_impact: None; correct build enables GPU acceleration.
works_for: Pip-installed PyTorch environments with CUDA mismatch.
Conda environments where CUDA packages conflict.
solutions.verification: torch.cuda.is_available() returns True and torch.version.cuda matches system capability.

solutions.quick_fix: Install a driver version that satisfies the CUDA compatibility matrix.
solutions.permanent_fix: Pin driver management in OS packaging or image build workflows.
steps: Identify current driver with nvidia-smi.
Check the minimum supported driver for the target CUDA version.
Install a newer NVIDIA driver from the official repository.
Reboot and verify nvidia-smi.
tradeoffs: New drivers can expose regressions on older GPUs.
solutions.performance_impact: None; may improve stability on newer hardware.
works_for: VMs with GPU passthrough but stale host drivers.
solutions.verification: Driver version meets or exceeds the CUDA runtime minimum.

solutions.permanent_fix: Configure the container runtime as the default GPU-aware runtime.
steps: Install the NVIDIA container toolkit.
Configure Docker runtime integration.
Restart Docker.
Test GPU visibility inside a CUDA container.
For Kubernetes, verify the NVIDIA device plugin is running.

solutions.quick_fix: Install the missing runtime libraries or use a CUDA image that already includes them.
solutions.permanent_fix: Use NVIDIA base images with validated CUDA and cuDNN stacks.
steps: Identify missing library dependencies with ldd.
Install cuDNN or CUDA runtime packages.
Set LD_LIBRARY_PATH if needed.
Prefer base images that include the full runtime stack.
solutions.performance_impact: None; these libraries are required for GPU execution.
solutions.verification: torch.backends.cudnn.version() or TensorFlow GPU listing succeeds.

solutions.quick_fix: Install a WSL2-capable NVIDIA driver on the Windows host.
solutions.permanent_fix: Use native Linux for production GPU workloads.
steps: Verify the host driver is WSL2-capable.
Confirm the WSL2 userspace library path is available.
Verify the CUDA library symlink if needed.
Test GPU detection from inside WSL2.
tradeoffs: Best-effort environment rather than a production-grade target.
solutions.performance_impact: Slight overhead relative to native Linux.
solutions.verification: nvidia-smi and framework GPU detection work inside WSL2.

verification_checklist.check: nvidia-smi output matches inside and outside container
verification_checklist.description: Container runtime correctly passes through GPU devices.

verification_checklist.check: Minimal CUDA kernel executes without error
verification_checklist.description: Runtime libraries are correctly linked and functional.

verification_checklist.check: Framework CUDA version matches system capability
verification_checklist.description: No binary incompatibility between framework build and driver.

verification_checklist.check: Training utilizes GPU memory and compute
verification_checklist.description: nvidia-smi shows GPU utilization during training.

practices: Pin CUDA version in requirements.txt or environment.yml and use lockfiles.
Always specify the CUDA-specific PyTorch wheel index for pip installs.
Test GPU detection in CI before launching full training jobs.
Use NVIDIA CUDA base images for reproducible environments.
Maintain a golden container image with a validated driver-CUDA-framework stack.
Pin NVIDIA driver versions in image or OS lifecycle management.
Run host and framework GPU preflight checks in job schedulers.
Document the CUDA compatibility matrix for each GPU node pool.
Alert when framework GPU detection is False on GPU-enabled nodes.
Track driver version drift across cluster nodes.
Monitor container runtime health on GPU worker nodes.
Log GPU utilization; zero utilization on GPU jobs indicates detection failure.
Always assert GPU availability before moving models to GPU.
Use explicit device selection with logging rather than silent fallback.
Fail fast instead of silently training on CPU.
Add environment validation to training script entrypoints.

common_misconceptions.misconception: nvidia-smi working means CUDA is fully functional
common_misconceptions.reality: nvidia-smi uses a different code path than CUDA runtime; the driver can be present while the framework build remains incompatible.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Installing CUDA toolkit is required for PyTorch GPU support
common_misconceptions.reality: PyTorch wheels often bundle the runtime they need; the problem is usually build/runtime mismatch, not a missing toolkit alone.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Latest driver always works with all CUDA versions
common_misconceptions.reality: Compatibility is bounded by supported driver/toolkit matrices.

false_positive_cases.how_to_distinguish: Code explicitly sets device='cpu'; CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="" is set.

false_positive_cases.case: Multi-GPU system where only some GPUs are allocated
false_positive_cases.why_it_looks_similar: torch.cuda.device_count() is less than the physical count.
false_positive_cases.how_to_distinguish: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set to a subset; nvidia-smi shows all GPUs.

false_positive_cases.case: GPU is in exclusive-process mode and occupied by another process
false_positive_cases.how_to_distinguish: nvidia-smi shows GPU in use by another process.

escalation_paths.when_to_use: Suspected hardware defect or driver bug.
tradeoffs: Response time may be several business days.

escalation_paths.when_to_use: Confirmed framework CUDA binding bug after isolation.
tradeoffs: Fix may not be available until a later release.

escalation_paths.when_to_use: Environment is irreparably corrupted by mixed installs or broken symlinks.
tradeoffs: Time-intensive but yields a clean state.
